strengths: The paper fills a genuine and clearly articulated gap: existing GMM-based cryo-EM reconstruction methods (E2GMM, CryoSTAR, DynaMight, etc.) all rely on externally computed consensus maps or atomic models for initialization, whereas cryoSplat demonstrates stable GMM optimization directly from raw particle images with random initialization. This is a meaningful foundational contribution for the field.

The technical adaptations are well-motivated and physically grounded: replacing alpha compositing with true line integrals, retaining the 1/(2π|Σ̃|^{1/2}) normalization term (which 3DGS omits), aligning the rasterization coordinate system with the FFT grid to avoid phase inconsistencies, and the unified learning rate across parameter types. The derivation from the image formation model (Eq. 1) through the closed-form orthographic projection of anisotropic Gaussians is clean and correct.

Evaluation on four real EMPIAR datasets with the standard gold-standard FSC protocol, spanning a range of difficulty (rigid ribosome to highly heterogeneous spliceosome), consistently shows improved or comparable resolution vs. backprojection and cryoDRGN, including notable gains on challenging heterogeneous datasets (2.49 Å vs 4.00/4.07 Å on EMPIAR-10049).

Useful ablations: number of Gaussians (Fig. 3, Fig. S2), isotropic vs. anisotropic Gaussians (Fig. S1), convergence behavior across epochs, runtime efficiency (Fig. 4), and GPU memory footprint (Table S1). The efficiency analysis (up to 30× speedup over cryoDRGN, sub-380 MiB memory) is convincing and practically relevant.
The appendix provides reasonable intuition for initialization and learning rate choices, and the paper is honest about its limitation (known poses, not ab initio).
weaknesses: Baseline coverage is thin. Only backprojection and cryoDRGN are compared. The justification that other neural methods 'differ mainly in pose estimation' is partially valid but incomplete; importantly, there is no comparison against the de facto standard production tools (RELION refinement, cryoSPARC) or against existing GMM-based methods (e.g., E2GMM) even in their intended regime. The claim of 'outperforming state-of-the-art methods' is therefore stronger than the evidence.

No synthetic-data experiments with ground-truth volumes. All evaluation relies on half-map FSC, which cannot detect systematic errors shared between half-maps (e.g., shared artifacts from incorrect poses or heterogeneity). Quantitative comparisons with ground truth (e.g., FSC against a reference model, or atomic-model validation) would substantially strengthen the claims.

FSC computation details are incomplete: no mention of solvent masking, mask correction, or phase randomization, which are standard practice and without which reported resolutions can be inflated. This affects the reported Ångström values for all methods, though presumably equally.

The improvement is not uniform: on EMPIAR-10028 (the cleanest dataset) cryoSplat only ties the baselines at 3.80 Å, and its advantage appears concentrated on datasets with heterogeneity or pose errors—i.e., settings where the homogeneous assumption is violated and where robustness claims are harder to attribute cleanly. A more careful analysis of why a homogeneous method is more 'robust to heterogeneity' (regularization effect of the GMM?) is missing.

Novelty is moderate: orthogonal projection of Gaussians is a classical, well-known closed-form operation (cited from Zwicker et al. 2002), and adapting 3DGS to a new domain is an increasingly common recipe. The FFT-grid half-pixel alignment and normalization fixes are sensible engineering but individually incremental; the main novelty is the combination and the demonstration that it converges from random initialization.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility for a paper whose central claim is a practical, self-contained reconstruction pipeline.

The MSE loss without any regularization on 30,000 freely optimized anisotropic Gaussians raises questions about overfitting to noise; the paper asserts stability 'in practice' but provides no analysis (e.g., of noise overfitting at higher frequencies) beyond FSC curves.

Some presentation issues: references with empty author fields ('(2021; 2023; 2023; 2024; 2024; 2025)') appear repeatedly in the text, which is unprofessional and hinders verification of the claims about prior work.

strengths: The paper is technically coherent: the real-space formulation (line-integral projection of anisotropic Gaussians, retained normalization, FFT-grid alignment) is carefully derived and the connection between 3DGS-style splatting and the cryo-EM orthographic projection model is clearly motivated.
A CUDA-accelerated renderer supporting tens of thousands of Gaussians is a nontrivial engineering contribution, with favorable runtime and memory results (Fig. 4, Table S1) compared to cryoDRGN.

The central claim of stable convergence from random initialization, previously unachieved for GMM-based cryo-EM reconstruction, is demonstrated across four real EMPIAR datasets with gold-standard FSC and convergence curves across epochs.

The paper includes useful ablations: number of Gaussians (Fig. 3, S2), isotropic vs. anisotropic Gaussians (Fig. S1), and justification of initialization and unified learning-rate choices in the appendix.
Limitations are acknowledged honestly: the method assumes known poses and does not qualify as ab initio reconstruction.
weaknesses: Scope of contribution is narrow. The method assumes known particle poses, so the task addressed is homogeneous reconstruction with poses given — essentially a solved problem that backprojection handles near-optimally. This limits the significance for a top-tier AI venue, and the paper's framing as filling a 'foundational gap' overstates the contribution.

The evaluation raises a validity concern: with poses known, backprojection is essentially the optimal linear estimator, yet the paper reports large FSC gains over it (e.g., 2.49 Å vs. 4.00 Å on EMPIAR-10049 — nearly the resolution of the published structure of that dataset). Half-map FSC can be inflated by implicit regularization or noise correlation between half-maps and does not establish accuracy against ground truth. No synthetic experiments with ground truth, no map-to-model validation (e.g., against deposited atomic models), and no cross-validation against a standard tool like RELION/cryoSPARC with the same poses are provided.

The baseline set is thin: only voxel backprojection and cryoDRGN. No comparison with other GMM-based methods (E2GMM, CryoSTAR, DynaMight) even in settings where they apply, and no heterogeneous or pose-estimation experiments despite these being the motivating applications.

Novelty is incremental: the core projection math is a direct application of Zwicker et al. (2002) EWA splatting with a normalization term, and the adaptations (half-pixel shift, unified learning rate, MSE loss) are engineering-level adjustments rather than conceptual advances.

Some design choices are justified only empirically or hand-wavily (e.g., the unified learning-rate argument in the appendix, the claim that MSE alone suffices without regularization), without ablations isolating each adaptation's contribution (normalization term, half-pixel alignment, etc.).
No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned, which is a significant drawback for a paper whose main value is an implementation (CUDA rasterizer) and empirical stability claims.

The 5-epoch training with exponential decay γ=0.1 appears aggressive; robustness of convergence across datasets, image sizes, and pose noise levels is only lightly explored, and only at downsampled resolutions (192–256 pixels).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: enabling self-contained GMM-based cryo-EM reconstruction from random initialization, filling a genuine gap since prior GMM methods (E2GMM, cryoSTAR, etc.) require consensus maps or atomic models for initialization.

Technically sound adaptation of Gaussian splatting to cryo-EM physics: the derived closed-form orthogonal projection of anisotropic Gaussians, retention of the normalization term (unlike 3DGS), half-pixel FFT grid alignment, and the physically grounded line-integral formulation replacing alpha blending are all carefully justified.

The explanation for using a unified learning rate across parameter types (avoiding gradient direction distortion) is a useful, non-obvious practical insight, and the real-space rasterization argument (locality of Gaussians in real vs. Fourier space) is convincing.

Solid experimental design for a homogeneous reconstruction method: gold-standard FSC on half-maps across four real EMPIAR datasets, epoch-by-epoch FSC curves demonstrating stable convergence from random initialization, ablations on the number of Gaussians and on isotropic vs. anisotropic Gaussians, plus runtime and GPU-memory comparisons (Table S1).

Efficiency results are meaningful: 2-3x higher FPS than cryoDRGN and up to ~30x overall speedup due to 5-epoch convergence, with very low memory footprint (<380 MiB), relevant for downstream heterogeneous analysis.
Honest limitation discussion: the authors correctly note that known poses prevent an ab initio claim, positioning the work as a foundation.
weaknesses: Scope is narrower than the framing suggests: the method assumes known particle poses and homogeneous structure, so the hard problems of cryo-EM (pose inference, ab initio reconstruction, heterogeneity) are not addressed; the 'first GMM method to reconstruct from scratch' claim is meaningful mainly within this restricted setting.

Missing the most relevant baselines: no quantitative comparison against prior GMM-based methods (e.g., E2GMM, cryoSTAR-style GMM variants) even in the known-pose setting they support; comparisons are limited to voxel backprojection and cryoDRGN, which weakens the central claim that prior GMM pipelines cannot work from scratch.

Evaluation relies solely on FSC self-consistency on real data; there are no synthetic experiments with ground-truth volumes, and no map-model validation against atomic structures. The large resolution gains (e.g., 2.49 A vs. 4.00-4.07 A on EMPIAR-10049) relative to established pipelines are surprisingly large and could partly reflect FSC inflation from overfitting or from GMM smoothing artifacts rather than genuinely better recovery of signal.

The claimed robustness to imperfect poses and heterogeneity (EMPIAR-10076, 10180) is not systematically quantified; datasets are known to be heterogeneous, and no experiments isolate the effect of pose error or mixing of states.

Novelty is largely an adaptation of 3DGS/Zwicker-style splatting: the projection math is standard (marginalization of Gaussians is classical), so the core contribution is more engineering-oriented than conceptually new; no ab initio or pose-estimation extension is demonstrated to show the framework's broader payoff.
Hyperparameter sensitivity is underexplored (single learning rate, fixed 5 epochs, exponential decay 0.1, fixed initialization statistics); no evidence of robustness to these choices across datasets.
No statement about code or renderer release, which limits reproducibility of the CUDA implementation, a central part of the contribution.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing GMM-based cryo-EM methods require external consensus maps or atomic models for initialization, and cryoSplat demonstrates stable reconstruction from random initialization with known poses, filling a genuine gap in the GMM-based reconstruction literature.

The technical adaptations (orthographic line-integral projection instead of alpha blending, retained 2D normalization term, FFT-aligned rasterization coordinates, unified learning rate) are physically principled and well-justified, with the real-space vs. Fourier-space rasterization rationale (Appendix A) being a nice argument for tile-based splatting.

Comprehensive ablations: number of Gaussians across regimes (64 to 524k), isotropic vs. anisotropic Gaussians, SNR robustness on synthetic data, initialization sensitivity across seeds and spreads, and a corrected-FSC analysis (Appendix D.4) that proactively addresses overfitting/self-consistency concerns.
Significant efficiency gains: ~30x faster convergence than cryoDRGN, low GPU memory footprint (<380 MiB even at 30k Gaussians), enabled by a well-engineered CUDA rasterizer with re-derived gradients.
Honest limitations section acknowledging that known-pose homogeneous reconstruction does not constitute ab initio capability.
weaknesses: Narrow scope relative to the claims: the method requires published consensus poses and assumes homogeneity. Homogeneous reconstruction with known poses is a largely solved problem (voxel backprojection is fast and near-optimal); the claimed significance as a 'foundation for heterogeneous/ab initio pipelines' remains future work, so the demonstrated contribution is a representation choice rather than new reconstruction capability.

Questionable fairness in the headline evaluation: baselines use a spherical mask for FSC while cryoSplat uses unmasked FSC (Appendix C.3), which can inflate cryoSplat's resolution estimates. Moreover, the default exponential decay (γ=0.1) is shown in the authors' own corrected-FSC analysis to overestimate resolution, yet the headline numbers in Fig. 2 (e.g., 2.49 Å vs. 4.07/4.23 Å on EMPIAR-10049) presumably use this setting; all comparisons should be re-reported at the bias-free γ=0.5 configuration.

Limited baselines: only cryoSPARC backprojection and cryoDRGN are compared. No comparison against other Gaussian/GMM-based methods (e.g., hierarchical GMM approaches by Shekarforoush et al., which target closely related problems and are cited but not compared), limiting the evidence for 'outperforming state-of-the-art methods.'

The novelty is incremental from a technical standpoint: the core projection math follows directly from Zwicker et al. (2002) EWA splatting, and the contributions are largely careful engineering adaptations (coordinate shift, normalization retention, learning-rate unification) rather than fundamentally new methodology.
No heterogeneous reconstruction or pose-estimation experiments despite these being the motivating applications; all four real datasets are standard, well-studied benchmarks.

Reproducibility is not yet demonstrated: the code is only promised for release, and several nontrivial implementation choices (initialization statistics, γ schedule) critically affect the reported results, as the paper's own ablations show.

strengths: The paper is clearly written, and the technical formulation (Sec. 3, Appendix A) is correct and complete: the closed-form orthographic projection of anisotropic Gaussians, the view-dependent normalization term retained from the physically meaningful density model, and the FFT-aligned rasterization grid (Fig. 5b, Eq. 13) are well motivated and carefully derived.

The CUDA tile-based rasterization adapted to cryo-EM, with removal of alpha blending in favor of direct summation consistent with the transmission model, is a sensible and well-executed engineering contribution with strong runtime and memory results (Fig. 4, Table 1).

The experimental section is unusually thorough for this problem area: ablations over Gaussian counts (including extreme regimes of 64 and 524k Gaussians), isotropic vs. anisotropic comparison, SNR stress tests on synthetic data, initialization-seed robustness (10 seeds), and an honest corrected-FSC analysis (Appendix D.4) that acknowledges the potential for half-map FSC to overestimate resolution.
Convergence within 5 epochs and low memory footprint represent a genuine practical improvement over cryoDRGN-style neural field optimization.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated. The paper is framed as a 'self-contained,' 'first' GMM method reconstructing 'directly from raw cryo-EM particle images... without external priors,' yet all experiments use published consensus poses and CTF parameters from prior work (Zhong et al. 2021a). With fixed poses, the problem reduces to weighted least-squares density fitting — a refinement task, not the ab initio reconstruction the framing implies. The limitation section (Sec. 5) admits this, but the abstract, introduction, and contributions do not, which is misleading.

Novelty is modest for a top-tier venue. Orthographic projection of anisotropic Gaussians yielding 2D Gaussians is classical (Zwicker et al. 2002, cited by the authors themselves), CTF modulation in Fourier space is entirely standard in cryo-EM, and the tile-based rasterizer is a direct adaptation of Kerbl et al. (2023). The remaining contributions — fixing per-type learning rates, a half-pixel FFT alignment, and a unified learning rate — are incremental heuristics rather than a principled methodological advance.

The headline quantitative claims rest on a metric the authors themselves show to be unreliable. Appendix D.4 demonstrates that the half-map FSC overestimates cryoSplat's resolution (corrected FSC exceeds half-map FSC at gamma=0.1), and the reported 'better than cryoSPARC' resolutions (e.g., 2.49 A on EMPIAR-10049, better than the published map) should be treated with skepticism. The resolution that 'corrects' the discrepancy (gamma=0.5) is effectively a tunable hyperparameter chosen post hoc.

Evaluation protocol is not fully fair across methods: baselines are evaluated with a spherical mask while cryoSplat uses unmasked FSC (Appendix C.3), justified by an assertion that masking has no effect. Given that FSC differences between methods are the core evidence, this asymmetry should have been eliminated or shown to be immaterial on the baselines themselves.

Missing baselines weaken the empirical case. No comparison to other continuous-representation refinement approaches operating under the same known-pose setting (e.g., GMM refinement from a consensus map, which is the natural strong baseline for this task), and heterogeneous-capable methods are excluded by fiat. The claim of 'outperforming state-of-the-art' is thus restricted to two baselines under a setting where the pose is given for free.

The significance of the contribution is limited by its own stated scope: because poses must be known, cryoSplat cannot serve as a standalone reconstruction tool, and its value as a 'foundation' for future ab initio or heterogeneous pipelines remains speculative. For a 30%-acceptance venue, a homogeneous-refinement renderer with an incrementally modified rasterizer, evaluated with contestable FSC numbers, is not sufficiently compelling.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: existing GMM-based cryo-EM methods require external consensus maps or atomic models for initialization, and the paper convincingly identifies this gap and addresses it with a self-contained pipeline starting from random initialization.

Physically grounded adaptation of Gaussian splatting: replacing alpha blending with orthographic line integrals, retaining the view-dependent normalization term, and aligning the rasterization coordinate system with the FFT grid are principled and clearly justified modifications, not naive transplantation of 3DGS.

Comprehensive experimental validation on four real EMPIAR datasets with gold-standard FSC evaluation, plus extensive ablations (number of Gaussians, isotropic vs. anisotropic, initialization robustness across seeds and spreads, SNR robustness on synthetic data, low/ultra-high Gaussian count regimes).

Honest and careful self-assessment of evaluation pitfalls: the corrected-FSC analysis (Appendix D.4) proactively investigates potential self-consistency bias in half-map FSC, which many papers in this area neglect.

Useful efficiency analysis: runtime (up to ~30x speedup over cryoDRGN), GPU memory footprint, and convergence speed (5 epochs vs. 50) are all quantified, demonstrating practical value of the CUDA rasterizer.
Clear presentation, complete derivation of gradients including the normalization term, and detailed algorithms supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scope of contribution is narrower than the framing suggests: the method assumes known particle poses and CTF parameters, so despite the 'ab initio'-adjacent claims in the introduction, it is not a fully self-supervised reconstruction method. The limitation is acknowledged only in the conclusion, and the significance of 'first GMM method from random initialization' is diminished since pose estimation—arguably the harder problem—is delegated to external tools.

Comparison fairness concerns: FSC curves for baselines use a spherical mask while cryoSplat uses unmasked FSC (Appendix C.3). Although the authors argue masks have little effect, this asymmetry could favor cryoSplat and should have been validated directly on the baselines in the main comparison.

Resolution gains may partly reflect the low-pass denoising nature of GMM representations rather than superior reconstruction; the paper itself notes FSC may overestimate resolution for cryoSplat, and no external metric (e.g., model-to-map fit, atomic model validation) corroborates the reported improvements.

Baseline coverage is limited: only cryoSPARC backprojection and cryoDRGN are compared; other relevant GMM-based or Fourier-domain neural methods are dismissed on the grounds that they differ in pose estimation, but a pose-controlled comparison with at least one additional modern baseline would strengthen the claims.
Some hyperparameters require per-setting tuning (e.g., the exponential decay γ raised to 0.5 in the ultra-high Gaussian regime), and the sensitivity/selection protocol for γ is not fully specified.

Novelty is primarily in careful engineering and adaptation rather than fundamentally new theory: the projection of anisotropic Gaussians is standard (Zwicker et al., 2002), and the main intellectual contributions (normalization retention, FFT alignment, unified learning rates) are individually modest.
